Effects of acoustic environment on design work performance based on
multitask visual cognitive performance in office space
Qi Meng, Yuying An, Da Yang*
Key Laboratory of Cold Region Urban and Rural Human Settlement Environment Science and Technology, Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, School of
Architecture, Harbin Institute of Technology, China
A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T
Keywords: The acoustic environment in the office space is a significant factor affecting workers’ performance. Whereas
Office existing research focuses mainly on the impact of the acoustic environment on single visual cognitive work
Acoustic environment performance, this study considers multitask visual cognitive work. Forty-one respondents were selected to
Multitask participate in the multitask visual cognitive–behavioural cognitive experiment under different acoustic envi-
Design visual cognition
ronments. The effects of different typical sound source types, sound pressure levels, and reverberation times on
Work performance
the performance of multitask visual cognition in design offices were examined. The results revealed the
following. First, the sound source types have a significant impact on the reaction time of participants’ work
performance. Compared to the ambient environment (mean =2.838 s), the reaction time performance is shortest
under music sound (mean = 2.560 s). Second, the increase in traffic noise and air-conditioning noise will
significantly reduce the memory accuracy of the location. For instance, when the traffic noise increases from 50
dBA to 65 dBA, the memory accuracy of the location is reduced by 4.42%. Third, the increase in the rever-
beration of speech will effectively shorten the reaction time and increase the memory accuracy of graphics. As
the reverberation time of speech increases from 0.3 s to 1.5 s, the reaction time is reduced by 0.274 s. Meanwhile,
2.03% of the memory accuracy of graphics increased. Furthermore, the personal characteristics of the partici-
pants also affected visual cognitive work. Therefore, it is expected to improve the visual cognitive work per-
formance of employees for room acoustic design.

2.6. Data analysis
The professional statistics commercial software SPSS 23.0 (Statistical
Product and Service Solutions, IBM, America) was used to conduct sta-
tistical analysis based on the data obtained from the experiment. Data
analysis used mainly the following four methods:
(1) The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (K–S test) was used to analyse the
normality of the experimental data.
(2) The nonparametric Kruskal-Wallis test was used to analyse the
differences between groups of experimental data under tesdif-
ferent sound source types. If p < 0.05, Nemenyi’s method would
be employed to conduct multiple comparison analyses on specific
differences between sound sources.
(3) The Spearman correlation analysis method was used to analyse
the correlation among SPL, RT, reaction time, and accuracy rate.
(4) The Mann-Whitney U Test was employed to test the impact of
respondents’ demographic characteristics on their visual cogni-
tive work performance.

The results showed that different sound sources had significant ef-
fects on participants’ visual cognitive work performance. Compared to
ambient sound environments, music and traffic noise effectively short-
ened the reaction time and promoted visual cognitive work perfor-
mance. In contrast, speech significantly interfered with the respondents’
visual cognitive work performance, followed by natural sounds. These
two types of sound sources increased the respondents’ reaction time and
reduced the memory accuracy of the location. This is contrary to the
original experimental hypothesis that natural sound would promote
visual cognitive work performance, while traffic noise would interfere
with the respondents’ visual cognitive work performance. The reason
may be that natural sound can effectively alleviate work pressure and
cause problems such as inattention [59]. In addition, noise can actively
strengthen the concentration ability and resistance to noise interference
in humans [60].
